TeamCity On-Premises server (java/Tomcat) spawning OS command interpreter — CVE-2026-63077 RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-63077: the TeamCity On-Premises server process (its bundled JRE / Tomcat catalina java process) spawning cmd/powershell/bash/discovery LOLBins. Builds run on agents, never on the server, so the server java process launching an OS shell is a high-fidelity RCE signal. Explicitly excludes the co-located build-agent process to avoid legitimate build-step noise. Rationale: Anchors on the article's confirmed mechanic — CVE-2026-63077 executes 'arbitrary OS commands with the privileges of the server process' via the agent polling protocol — by matching the TeamCity server's bundled java/catalina parent (cmdline contains TeamCity) spawning shells/LOLBins, while excluding buildAgent since legitimate build steps run on agents not the server. Cross-checked JetBrains advisory, Rapid7, Help Net Security and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63077-critical-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-in-jetbrains-teamcity/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/28/teamcity-rce-cve-2026-63077-fixed/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-teamcity-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TeamCity server and build agent installed on the same host, where the agent's java process runs build steps that shell out (mitigated by the buildAgent exclusion)
  • Sysadmin running diagnostic commands under the TeamCity service account on the server host
  • Server-side VCS/plugin tooling that legitimately shells out (rare; typically git.exe/svn.exe which are not in the child list)
  • Monitoring/backup agents invoked via the Tomcat service wrapper
  • Custom server-side health-check scripts launched from teamcity-server.bat startup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent" and not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("teamcity-server.bat","runAll.bat","service.bat","wrapper"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the parent is the TeamCity SERVER java process (cmdline has TeamCity + catalina/Bootstrap and NOT buildAgent) and inspect the child command line for recon (whoami/net/nltest) or download (certutil/curl) intent; capture SHA256 and check TeamCity server version against 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3. 2) Contain: Network-isolate the TeamCity host, rotate all credentials stored in TeamCity (VCS tokens, cloud keys, artifact-repo creds — assume exposed per advisory), and take the server offline from the internet. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the host for outbound C2 from the java/child process, new admin users or tokens in TeamCity, tampered build configs/artifacts, and repeat the query across all TeamCity server hosts for lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "TeamCity"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina","Bootstrap","teamcity-server")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent"   // builds run on the AGENT, not the server
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh","bash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","reg.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has "java"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "TeamCity"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina","Bootstrap","teamcity-server")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","whoami","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","curl","wget","bitsadmin.exe","nltest.exe","reg.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentImage = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamCity Server Process Spawning OS Command Interpreter (CVE-2026-63077 RCE)
id: b3d9f0a2-1c4e-4a7b-9e21-7f2c6a8d5e10
status: experimental
description: Detects the TeamCity On-Premises server (bundled JRE / Tomcat java) spawning an OS shell or discovery LOLBin, the post-exploitation footprint of the CVE-2026-63077 unauthenticated deserialization RCE. Builds execute on agents, so the server java process launching a shell is anomalous.
references:
  - https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/
  - https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63077-critical-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-in-jetbrains-teamcity/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\javaw.exe'
      - '\tomcat9.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'TeamCity'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\whoami.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\net1.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\nltest.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
  filter_agent:
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'buildAgent'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and not filter_agent
falsepositives:
  - Administrator or monitoring scripts launched under the TeamCity service account
  - Server-side maintenance tooling invoked via the service wrapper
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\java.exe OR *\\javaw.exe OR *\\Java.exe) @ParentCommandLine:(*TeamCity* OR *teamcity*) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\Cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\nltest.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\wscript.exe) -@ParentCommandLine:*buildAgent*

| ParentImageFileName=/teamcity/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|whoami|net|net1|certutil|curl|wget|bitsadmin|nltest|cscript|wscript)\.exe$/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/buildAgent/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Unpatched internet-facing TeamCity On-Premises exposed to CVE-2026-63077 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces TeamCity On-Premises hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-63077 (all versions below 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3), prioritising internet-facing servers. Because the flaw is unauthenticated and CVSS 9.8, exposure inventory is the fastest path to shrinking the attack surface before exploitation. Article-specific: keys directly on the CVE ID and vendor-named fixed versions. Rationale: Uses the two article-confirmed facts — CVE-2026-63077 and the fixed versions 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3 with 'all versions affected' — to enumerate exposed TeamCity servers, joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to prioritise the unauthenticated-HTTP attack path the advisory calls out. Verified against JetBrains, Rapid7, and SecurityWeek. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63077-critical-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-in-jetbrains-teamcity/ • https://www.securityweek.com/critical-code-execution-vulnerability-patched-in-teamcity/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Server already patched via the security-patch plugin but TVM still keys on the base version number (plugin patches without version bump — verify plugin install state)
  • TeamCity Cloud agents mislabeled as On-Premises (Cloud is not affected per advisory)
  • Decommissioned/offline TeamCity hosts still present in the vuln inventory
  • Non-production/lab TeamCity instances on isolated segments flagged as internet-facing by stale network data
  • TVM version-detection lag immediately after an in-progress upgrade to 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName has "TeamCity" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "2025.11.7" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "2026.1.3"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Rank hits by IsInternetFacing=true, then confirm each host's TeamCity version and whether the CVE-2026-63077 security-patch plugin is installed (plugin fixes without a version bump, so cross-check plugin state, not just version string). 2) Contain: For any internet-facing unpatched server, place it behind VPN/WAF or restrict the login page + REST API by source IP immediately (per JetBrains best-practice guidance) and schedule emergency upgrade to 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3. 3) Hunt: On every exposed host, run the companion RCE detection (server java spawning a shell) over the exposure window and review TeamCity audit logs / stored-credential access for signs the flaw was already exploited before patching.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-63077"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo

    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
    | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          RecommendedSecurityUpdate, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel,
          IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, CveId
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

  ) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          RecommendedSecurityUpdate, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel,
          IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, CveId
| order by IsInternetFacing desc

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-63077")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-63077")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-63077")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

AWS Amplify UI Builder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent — CVE-2025-4318 malicious schema injection AIInstallation Medium
Hunts AmplifyUIBuilder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent CloudTrail events, the exact API path an authenticated principal uses to import a component schema whose property bindings carry arbitrary JavaScript (CVE-2025-4318). The injected expression re-executes during every codegen/render/build, so the create/update call is the persistence-planting event to surface and attribute to a principal + source IP. Rationale: Uses the concrete eventSource amplifyuibuilder.amazonaws.com and the CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent API names named in the advisory (and confirmed in the AmplifyUIBuilder API reference) — the exact and only path a malicious component schema is imported through. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react/CVE-2025-4318/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers building/editing UI Builder components in Amplify Studio during normal front-end development
  • Amplify Studio auto-generating components from a DataStore/GraphQL schema import
  • CI service role programmatically syncing components as part of an IaC/export workflow
  • QA or design teams iterating on forms/views/themes
  • First-time Amplify Studio onboarding generating starter components in bulk
Suppression filter
| where userIdentity.type != "AssumedRole" or requestParameters.name has_any ("eval","constructor","process","require","${")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress and componentName; confirm the principal is an expected Amplify developer and the IP/geo matches normal dev activity. Retrieve the component schema (GetComponent) and inspect bindingProperties/collectionProperties for expression-like or JS payloads (e.g. constructor, process, require, backtick/${} expressions). 2) Contain: if the schema contains code, delete/roll back the component, rotate the principal's credentials, and freeze codegen builds that pull it (amplify pull / ampx) until packages are on @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) >= 2.20.4. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CreateComponent/UpdateComponent by that principal, check build-host/CI process telemetry for anomalous node child processes at codegen time, and inventory repos for vulnerable codegen-ui versions <=2.20.2.

AWS Amplify UI Builder create-component CLI invocation on endpoint/CI host (CVE-2025-4318) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts process executions of the AWS CLI 'amplifyuibuilder create-component/update-component/export-component' commands on developer workstations and CI/build runners — the client-side action that imports a component schema and (for vulnerable <=2.20.2 codegen-ui) triggers arbitrary JavaScript during local codegen/build. Complements the CloudTrail UC by catching the on-host command line and its parent process. Rationale: Anchors on the exact 'create-component' command named in the advisory (plus the update/export variants that share the vulnerable binding path) scoped by the 'amplifyuibuilder' service token, so it fires only on Amplify UI Builder schema imports rather than generic AWS CLI usage. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Front-end developers legitimately importing/exporting components via aws amplifyuibuilder in local dev
  • CI/CD pipeline steps that scriptaws amplifyuibuilder export-component for codegen
  • Infrastructure-as-code sync jobs recreating components from JSON definitions
  • Amplify migration/backup scripts bulk-exporting components
  • Automated tests that provision throwaway components
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jenkins-agent.exe","runner.worker.exe","buildkitd.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and any --cli-input-json / --component-to-create payload path; open the referenced schema and inspect property bindings for JS (eval, constructor, require, ${}, backticks). Confirm whether the host's node_modules ships @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) <=2.20.2. 2) Contain: on a confirmed malicious schema, isolate the build host/CI runner, kill child node/codegen processes, and block the build from publishing artifacts; upgrade codegen-ui to >=2.20.4 before re-running. 3) Hunt: correlate to the CloudTrail CreateComponent/UpdateComponent event by the same identity/time, review that principal's other Amplify actions, and sweep all build hosts for the vulnerable package version.

Compromised @joyfill npm bundle dropped in node_modules (2773 beta RAT) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the malicious @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts distribution bundles landing on disk under node_modules, matched by the article's payload SHA256 hashes and the exact dist file paths the RAT was injected into. Catches the supply-chain implant at install/checkout time on developer machines, CI runners, and repos. Rationale: Anchored on the three payload SHA256 hashes and the exact injected bundles named in the article (dist/index.js, index.esm.js, joyfill.min.js, index.cjs.js, index.es.js) under @joyfill node_modules — no legitimate release ships these hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://socket.dev/blog/polinrider-north-korea-linked-supply-chain-campaign-expands • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/

  • Internal artifact-mirror caching legitimate pre-July-28 @joyfill tarballs
  • Security team restoring the malicious sample into a sandbox for analysis
  • EDR re-scanning an existing node_modules tree during a full disk sweep

Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the SHA256 and file path — if hash matches, it is the confirmed implant; if only path matches, diff the bundle for the `9-0135-3` marker string. Identify the device (dev workstation vs CI runner). 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill node processes, and remove the 2773-beta versions; force re-pin to a @joyfill release published before 2026-07-28. 3. Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound to the C2 IPs (166.88.134.62 / 23.27.13.43 / 198.105.127.210 / 23.27.202.27), node -e children, and modified @vscode/deviceid, Discord, GitHub Desktop, or npm CLI modules; rotate every credential present on the machine.

@joyfill RAT C2 callout to hardcoded IPs / Socket.IO boot paths AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from developer/CI hosts to the four C2 IPs used by the @joyfill implant and to its distinctive request paths (/$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv). This is the Socket.IO RAT channel and the second-stage /$/boot downloader described in the article. Rationale: Uses the four verbatim C2 IPs and the six exact RAT request paths from the article's IOC block; these are static infrastructure indicators with essentially no benign use.   • A pentest replaying these IOCs during an authorized supply-chain exercise
  • Proxy log noise where /snv or /u/f appears in an unrelated legitimate API path (mitigated by pairing with the IPs)

Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe (or a dev tool bundling Node) and whether the destination is one of the four hardcoded IPs vs only a path match. 2. Contain: block the four C2 IPs at the egress proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and terminate Node processes. 3. Hunt: correlate with @joyfill bundle presence (UC1), node -e children hitting /$/boot, and outbound to the blockchain resolver hosts; treat all workstation credentials/tokens as exposed and rotate.

Node.js resolving C2 via blockchain dead-drop (Tron/BSC/Aptos RPC) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for a Node.js process on a workstation or CI runner reaching public blockchain RPC endpoints (api.trongrid.io, bsc-dataseed.binance.org, bsc-rpc.publicnode.com, fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com) — the @joyfill implant's dead-drop resolver that reads a Tron transaction and follows it to a BSC transaction to decode its live C2. Blockchain RPC from a build/dev Node process is highly abnormal. Rationale: Uses the exact blockchain RPC hostnames named in the article's lookup-endpoint IOCs, scoped to a Node.js initiating process so legitimate wallet/crypto apps on the same host don't fire. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately building or testing a web3/dApp project that uses trongrid or bsc-dataseed via Node
  • CI job running blockchain integration tests against public RPC endpoints
  • A crypto-price widget or wallet SDK bundled into an Electron dev tool making these lookups
  • Corporate proxy collapsing the initiating process so node scoping is lost (widen review manually)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hardhat","truffle","web3","ethers","@tronweb","foundry") )
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the Node process is not part of a known web3 project in that repo — check the working directory / command line and the presence of @joyfill in node_modules. 2. Contain: if @joyfill or the C2 IPs are also present, isolate the host and kill node; otherwise annotate as likely-benign web3 dev. 3. Hunt: look for the follow-on eval-based execution and outbound to the four C2 IPs on the same host within minutes of the RPC lookup.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js spawning detached 'node -e' second-stage child (/$/boot loader) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a node.exe process spawning another node.exe with an inline `-e` script — the @joyfill implant's detached second stage that requests /$/boot from a second host and XOR-decrypts the response, running independently of the Socket.IO channel. Inline eval children of Node are rare on developer endpoints. Rationale: Targets the article's described 'detached node -e child that requests /$/boot' — the node→node -e parent/child shape plus the /$/boot path is a specific behavioural fingerprint, not a generic Node launch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tooling (webpack/vite/jest workers) that legitimately forks node with -e for worker bootstrapping
  • nvm / npx wrapper scripts invoking node --eval
  • Monorepo task runners (turbo, nx) spawning inline-eval node helpers
  • A developer manually running node -e for a quick one-liner
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("webpack","vite","jest-worker","turbo","nx","ts-node","npx") and not ProcessCommandLine has "/$/boot")
Response runbook
1. Triage: read the child's full command line — a genuine build worker will reference a project path; the implant references /$/boot or an opaque XOR/eval blob. 2. Contain: if the command line contains /$/boot or unreadable eval content, isolate the host and kill both node processes. 3. Hunt: check the same host for @joyfill bundles, blockchain RPC lookups, and outbound to 23.27.13.43 (the /$/boot server); rotate credentials.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" and FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" -e ","--eval") or ProcessCommandLine has "/$/boot"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe" and ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (" -e ","--eval") or ActingProcessCommandLine has "/$/boot"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="node.exe" Processes.process_name="node.exe" (Processes.process="* -e *" OR Processes.process="*--eval*" OR Processes.process="*/$/boot*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
@joyfill RAT persistence: Node rewriting VS Code / Discord / GitHub Desktop / npm modules AIInstallation High
Detects node.exe modifying the developer-tool modules the @joyfill implant hijacks for persistence — @vscode/deviceid (used by VS Code, Cursor, Antigravity), the Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI — into which it inserts a self-reloading block. These files are not normally rewritten by a Node process. Rationale: Directly enumerates the four persistence targets named in the article (@vscode/deviceid, Discord desktop core, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI) and requires a node/npm writer — legitimate installers use msiexec/updater processes, not node rewriting these in place. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://socket.dev/blog/polinrider-north-korea-linked-supply-chain-campaign-expands
ATT&CKT1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate `npm install -g` upgrading the global npm CLI (writes npm-cli.js via node)
  • VS Code / Cursor auto-update rewriting bundled @vscode/deviceid
  • Discord client self-update repackaging discord_desktop_core
  • GitHub Desktop applying its own squirrel auto-update to main.js
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install -g","npm-upgrade","update-notifier") and FileName =~ "npm-cli.js")
Response runbook
1. Triage: inspect the modifying node/npm command line and diff the touched module for an injected self-reloading block or the `9-0135-3` marker; a legit updater will be an official installer/updater process chain, not an ad-hoc node from a project dir. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill node, and restore the affected modules from a clean install of VS Code/Discord/GitHub Desktop/npm. 3. Hunt: pivot to @joyfill bundle presence, C2 IP callouts, and the Python stealer's collection of browser/wallet/Git credentials; rotate all developer credentials and tokens on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\@vscode\deviceid\"
     or FolderPath has "discord_desktop_core"
     or (FolderPath has "GitHub Desktop" and FileName =~ "main.js")
     or FileName =~ "npm-cli.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\@vscode\deviceid\"
     or TargetFilePath has "discord_desktop_core"
     or (TargetFilePath has "GitHub Desktop" and TargetFileName =~ "main.js")
     or TargetFileName =~ "npm-cli.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |

    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase

    - attack.execution

            - 'Invoke-Expression'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised npm Packages: @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts Ship an Obfus Exploitation High

Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the core arbitrary-file-read primitive of CVE-2026-66066: a crafted upload drives an unfuzzed libvips loader inside the Ruby/Puma process to read the process environment and Rails secrets (secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc). Because libvips is linked into the app process, the read shows up as the web-app binary opening files it never touches at runtime. Rationale: Anchored on the exact read targets the GHSA names as the payoff (secret_key_base in the process environment, master.key, credentials.yml.enc) and scoped to the Ruby web-app process as the actor — that pairing is the file-read primitive itself, not a generic file-access rule. Confirmed via the advisory plus Ethiack and Flatt write-ups that the impact is disclosure of the process environment. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails • https://www.libvips.org/2022/05/28/What's-new-in-8.13.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately reading config/master.key and config/credentials.yml.enc at boot (normal startup — not /proc/self/environ)
  • Backup or DLP agents reading /etc/passwd during scheduled scans
  • APM/observability agents (e.g. Datadog, New Relic) reading /proc/<pid>/environ for metadata enrichment
  • Config-management runs (Ansible/Chef) reading /etc/passwd or .env files
  • Container init scripts sourcing .env files at container start
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("rails server","puma","bootsnap"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the actor is the web-app process (ruby/puma) and the read occurred mid-request (not at process start) — correlate the read timestamp against Active Storage variant/representation requests in the web/access log. 2) Contain: if /proc/self/environ or /etc/passwd was read by the app process, treat secret_key_base and every env-resident credential as exposed — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB creds and S3/GCS/Azure Active Storage keys immediately (invalidates sessions). 3) Hunt: check for follow-on ruby-spawned shells and outbound connections from the host, and search web logs for the uploads that preceded the read (/rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads).

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/proc/self/environ","/environ","/etc/passwd","/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc","/.env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the RCE stage of CVE-2026-66066: after leaking secret_key_base, the attacker forges a signed/encrypted Rails cookie carrying a deserialization payload, yielding code execution inside the app process. Surfaces the anomalous child — an interactive shell or download tool spawned by the Ruby/Puma web worker. Rationale: The advisory states the file-read escalates to RCE via secrets in the process environment; the observable outcome is the Rails worker (ruby/puma/passenger) spawning a shell or fetch tool — a parent→child pair that is abnormal for a web app running the in-process :vips processor. Parents and children are all concrete binary names, no placeholders. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails apps that legitimately shell out via system()/backticks (e.g. running git, imagemagick/mini_magick, ffmpeg, or a rake task)
  • Deploy/boot scripts where puma is launched by a shell wrapper and re-execs sh
  • Health-check or cron jobs invoking curl/wget from within the app container
  • Background job workers (Sidekiq/Resque under ruby) shelling out to CLI tools by design
  • Container entrypoints where bundle exec spawns sh for pre-boot hooks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i ","sh -c","bash -c","-c 'curl","-c \"curl","base64 -d") or ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("git","convert","mogrify","ffmpeg","rake")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp, -i, bash -c with piped curl) or interactive shells with no args are high-confidence; benign shell-outs name a specific tool/arg. Correlate against UC1 file-read hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host/pod, kill the offending Ruby worker, and rotate secret_key_base + all env-resident credentials (the RCE path depends on the leaked signing key). 3) Hunt: pull the preceding web requests to /rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, review outbound connections from the host, and check for persistence (cron, authorized_keys, new services).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","ruby3.2","ruby3.3","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt for the attack surface: hosts with an activestorage version affected by CVE-2026-66066 (< 7.2.3.2, 8.0.x < 8.0.5.1, 8.1.x < 8.1.3.1), prioritising internet-facing systems and those still on libvips < 8.13 which cannot block unfuzzed loaders. Drives patch/mitigation before the 2026-08-28 full disclosure. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the vendor-published affected-version boundaries from the advisory; joining internet-facing status turns a raw inventory list into a ranked remediation queue for the specific gem in this CVE. No version-string math needed — the TVM CveId already encodes the affected ranges. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 7.2.3.2 / 8.0.5.1 / 8.1.3.1 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale)
  • Apps that carry ruby-vips only for image analysis and never generate variants (lower real risk despite matching)
  • Hosts where libvips >= 8.13 is present and VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true) is already set (mitigated without gem upgrade)
  • Non-production/staging boxes flagged as internet-facing by network heuristics but actually firewalled
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm variant_processor is :vips (default since load_defaults 7.0) and whether the app accepts uploads from untrusted users — those two conditions gate real exploitability. 2) Contain: upgrade activestorage to the fixed release and ensure libvips >= 8.13; where an immediate upgrade isn't possible, set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED=1 (or Vips.block_untrusted(true)) as an interim block, prioritising internet-facing hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that was exposed before patching, assume secret exposure — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB and Active Storage service credentials, and run UC1/UC2 retrospectively over the exposure window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DPRK-Linked macOS Malvertising Uses Fake Updates to Deliver Crypto-Stealing Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 20 use cases 13 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A lot of security still comes down to trusting the wrong screen. This week, that screen might be a login page, an install guide, a recruiter call, or a familiar service behaving slightly wrong. Behind it: reused credentials, exposed systems, quiet loaders, abused trust, and exploit paths that should have been harder. Some defenses improved. The loose parts still got found first. Anyway,

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] MacSync fake-Claude Terminal one-liner: curl piped to zsh via base64 -D · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ClickFix rundll32 ordinal (#1) execution of non-DLL payload over WebDAV @SSL · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MacSync RAT C2 / wallet-exfil to 85.206.161.241 and agenticsora/malwareaudit infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] MacSync server-side AppleScript stealer: osascript, dscl authonly, keychain, ditto to /tmp/osalogging.zip · [LLM] MacSync wallet trojanization: app.asar swap + ad-hoc codesign of Ledger/Trezor apps · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
ClickFix rundll32 ordinal (#1) execution of non-DLL payload over WebDAV @SSL AIExploitation High
Hunts the CyberProof-tracked ClickFix variant where a pasted Run-dialog command mounts an attacker WebDAV share (\\host@SSL\GUID) and uses rundll32.exe to load a non-DLL file (gc.key, j.pm, goog.ct) by ordinal export #1. Article-specific because it keys on the payload filenames plus the rundll32 ',#1' + '@SSL' WebDAV UNC combination rather than generic rundll32 abuse. Rationale: Keys on the three verbatim payload filenames (gc.key/j.pm/goog.ct) and the rundll32 ',#1' ordinal-load plus '@SSL' WebDAV UNC syntax quoted in the CyberProof write-up — a combination that does not occur in benign rundll32 usage, which always references a real .dll by exported name. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/clickfix-keeps-evolving-rundll32-ordinal-execution-over-webdav/ • https://gbhackers.com/rundll32-and-webdav/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-clickfix-variant-uses-rundll32/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1204.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers that call rundll32 with a real DLL export happen to contain the literal token '#1' in an unrelated argument (rare — no @SSL/payload-name overlap)
  • Internal red-team / purple-team ClickFix simulations reusing the public payload names
  • Security tooling detonating the sample in a sandbox that shares the production Defender workspace
  • A file share genuinely named with '@SSL' in its path (uncommon; WebDAV-over-HTTPS UNC is almost never used interactively)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "@SSL" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("gc.key","j.pm","goog.ct"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain (explorer.exe->powershell/pcalua/cmd->rundll32). Extract the WebDAV host from the '\\host@SSL' UNC and the payload filename; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the 443/WebDAV connection to that host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block the WebDAV domain at proxy/DNS, and kill/quarantine any child processes rundll32 spawned. Reset the user's credentials if hands-on-keyboard follow-on is seen. 3) HUNT: Sweep the org for rundll32 loading any non-.dll file by ordinal '#1', for WebClient service starts, and for the same WebDAV domains across all endpoints; review clipboard/Run-dialog (RunMRU) history on the victim.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "#1"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gc.key", "j.pm", "goog.ct") or ProcessCommandLine has "@SSL"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine has "#1"
| where CommandLine has_any ("gc.key", "j.pm", "goog.ct") or CommandLine has "@SSL"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ClickFix Rundll32 Ordinal Execution of Non-DLL Payload over WebDAV

MacSync fake-Claude Terminal one-liner: curl piped to zsh via base64 -D AIDelivery High
Hunts the Huntress-documented MacSync initial-access step where a victim pastes a Terminal one-liner (curl -kfsSL $(echo <b64>|base64 -D)|zsh) that resolves to agenticsora[.]com or malwareaudit[.]com /curl/<token> and executes the stage-1 zsh loader. Article-specific because it pins on the exact delivery domains and the base64-decode-then-pipe-to-zsh shape rather than generic curl usage. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim delivery domains (agenticsora[.]com, malwareaudit[.]com) from the Huntress reversing plus the distinctive 'curl ... $(...|base64 -D)|zsh' construction — legitimate macOS install guides fetch signed .dmg/.pkg files, they do not base64-decode a URL and pipe HTTP to the shell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fake-claude-code-install-guide/ • https://gbhackers.com/fake-claude-code-installer-3/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using curl|zsh for a trusted install script (e.g. Homebrew, oh-my-zsh) — excluded by the domain/base64-decode anchors
  • Internal macOS provisioning tooling that pipes remote scripts to a shell (should not reference the attacker domains)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the MacSync sample
  • CI runners on macOS fetching bootstrap scripts (won't match the specific domains or the base64 -D wrapper)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("brew.sh", "raw.githubusercontent.com", "install.sh") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("agenticsora.com","malwareaudit.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the full ProcessCommandLine and decode the base64 blob to confirm the /curl/<token> endpoint; check for the follow-on zsh loader and a persistence line appended to ~/.zshrc. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Mac, block agenticsora[.]com and malwareaudit[.]com at DNS/proxy, and kill the zsh/curl process tree. Treat all local secrets as compromised. 3) HUNT: On the host look for ~/.local/.mpwd, /tmp/osalogging.zip, LaunchAgents at ~/.local/com.apple.<hex>.hcpi.plist, and outbound to 85.206.161[.]241:8443; sweep other Macs for the same domains and Terminal-spawned curl|zsh.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl", "zsh", "sh", "bash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "base64 -D" and ProcessCommandLine has "zsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl", "zsh", "sh", "bash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "base64 -D" and ProcessCommandLine has "zsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync server-side AppleScript stealer: osascript, dscl authonly, keychain, ditto to /tmp/osalogging.zip AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts MacSync's stage-3 credential harvest: a server-side AppleScript pulled via curl '.../dynamic?txd=<token>' and run through osascript, password validation with 'dscl . authonly', Keychain Safe Storage extraction, and staging to /tmp/osalogging.zip via 'ditto -c -k'. Article-specific because it pins on the named staging archive, the authonly validation, and the osascript-from-curl chain. Rationale: Anchors on three verbatim MacSync artifacts from Huntress — the '.../dynamic?txd=' AppleScript fetch piped to osascript, 'dscl . authonly' password validation, and the '/tmp/osalogging.zip' ditto archive — none of which are typical of benign macOS admin activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/30/fake-claude-install-guide-delivers-six-stage-macos-stealer-and-rat-huntress-finds/
ATT&CKT1059.002 T1555.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MDM/admin scripts calling 'dscl . authonly' to validate a local password (rare and usually not paired with curl-fed osascript)
  • Backup or migration tooling using 'ditto -c -k' to archive folders (won't target /tmp/osalogging.zip)
  • Developer running an internal AppleScript via osascript (no 'dynamic?txd=' curl source)
  • Security product self-tests exercising Keychain access
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the osascript parent was a curl fetch to an attacker /dynamic endpoint; check whether /tmp/osalogging.zip, ~/.local/.mpwd, or /tmp/sync<rand>/ exist and were exfiltrated. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Mac; rotate every credential class the stealer touches — macOS login/Keychain, browser-stored passwords, SSH keys, cloud/Kubernetes tokens, Telegram sessions. 3) HUNT: Look for the RAT LaunchAgent (~/.local/com.apple.<hex>.hcpi.plist) and C2 to 85.206.161[.]241:8443, and sweep the fleet for osascript spawned by curl and for 'dscl . authonly' invocations.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "osascript" and (ProcessCommandLine has "dynamic?txd=" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "curl"))
    or (FileName =~ "dscl" and ProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (FileName =~ "ditto" and ProcessCommandLine has "osalogging.zip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "osascript" and (ProcessCommandLine has "dynamic?txd=" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "curl"))
    or (FileName =~ "dscl" and ProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (FileName =~ "ditto" and ProcessCommandLine has "osalogging.zip")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync RAT C2 / wallet-exfil to 85.206.161.241 and agenticsora/malwareaudit infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to MacSync's confirmed infrastructure: the Mach-O RAT C2 at 85.206.161[.]241:8443 (TLS/WebSocket) and the delivery/exfil domains agenticsora[.]com, malwareaudit[.]com, main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com, main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com. Article-specific because it uses the exact IP and domains corroborated in the Huntress reversing. Rationale: Uses the verbatim RAT C2 IP 85.206.161[.]241:8443 and the seed-phrase exfil domains (main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com, main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com) from the Huntress analysis, all present in the article's pre-extracted IOC set — direct atomic indicators with near-zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fake-claude-code-install-guide/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or sandbox infrastructure in the org intentionally beaconing to the IOC for validation
  • A domain being sinkholed/reassigned to a benign parking host after takedown (verify current resolution)
  • Proxy/EDR log replay or backfill re-surfacing historical detonation traffic
  • Vulnerability scanners probing the exfil domains as part of an IOC-coverage test
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection (expect the MacSync Mach-O RAT under ~/.local); confirm bytes-out to 85.206.161[.]241:8443 and any POSTs to the /modules/wallets exfil paths. 2) CONTAIN: Block the IP and all four domains at egress, isolate the host, and remove the RAT LaunchAgent persistence. 3) HUNT: Reverse-search the fleet for any host that resolved or connected to these indicators, and for the stage-1 curl|zsh delivery and /tmp/osalogging.zip staging on those hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.206.161.241"
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com", "main.sdhomeinspectors.com", "main.southcarolinacounselor.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.206.161.241"
    or Url has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com", "main.sdhomeinspectors.com", "main.southcarolinacounselor.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync wallet trojanization: app.asar swap + ad-hoc codesign of Ledger/Trezor apps AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts MacSync's stage-6 wallet tampering where installed wallet apps (Ledger Wallet/Live, Trezor Suite) are rewritten in place by swapping app.asar, injecting recovery-step-*.html phishing pages, and ad-hoc re-signing with 'codesign -f -s -'. Article-specific because it keys on modification of app.asar inside wallet bundles and the injected phishing filename pattern. Rationale: Targets the specific stage-6 artifacts Huntress documented — in-place app.asar replacement inside Ledger/Trezor bundles and injected 'recovery-step-*.html' seed-phrase phishing pages — a high-signal tamper pattern; medium FP because legitimate Electron wallet updates also rewrite app.asar, mitigated by the recovery-step filename and by pivoting on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://gbhackers.com/fake-claude-code-installer-3/
ATT&CKT1554 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Ledger Live / Trezor Suite auto-update rewriting its own app.asar (excluded when the writer is not the official updater or when recovery-step-* pages appear)
  • A developer rebuilding an Electron wallet app locally
  • MDM-pushed wallet app reinstall
  • Backup software restoring a wallet app bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Ledger Live", "Trezor Suite", "Squirrel", "com.apple.installer") and FileName !startswith "recovery-step-")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the process that wrote app.asar / recovery-step-* — if it is not the vendor's signed updater, treat as malicious; check for a preceding 'codesign -f -s -' ad-hoc re-sign of the wallet bundle. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the tampered wallet app, and warn the user NOT to enter seed phrases; assume any wallet accessed post-tamper is compromised and initiate fund migration to a clean wallet. 3) HUNT: Sweep for the injected recovery-step-* pages and POSTs to main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com / main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com /modules/wallets, plus the upstream curl|zsh MacSync delivery on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated")
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has_any ("Ledger", "Trezor"))
    or FileName startswith "recovery-step-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated")
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has_any ("Ledger", "Trezor"))
    or FileName startswith "recovery-step-"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
