Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Copilot for Word Can Copy Hidden Prompts Into New Documents

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 4 use cases 3 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Hidden instructions in a Word document can make Microsoft 365 Copilot rewrite figures in a report, then copy the same instructions into the finished file. Håkon Måløy disclosed the technique on July 28, 144 days after reporting it to Microsoft. In his proof of concept, the internally generated file triggered the same behavior when it was used in a second Copilot drafting session. Måløy's

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk persistence: 'GoogleUpDate' scheduled task executing Videos\1.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the OctLurk deployment technique where the actor creates a scheduled task named GoogleUpDate that runs, once, as SYSTEM, a batch script staged at C:\Users\<user>\Videos\1.bat. That batch script (MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a) creates the malicious service that side-loads the loader DLL. Article-specific because the task name masquerades as a Google updater but launches a .bat from the Videos folder — a combination legitimate updaters never use. Rationale: Anchors on two exact article strings: the task name 'GoogleUpDate' and the payload path '\Videos\1.bat' (MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a). A batch file in a media folder driven by a fake Google-update task is unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google Update tasks are named 'GoogleUpdateTaskMachine*' and run GoogleUpdate.exe from Program Files — never a .bat in Videos, so overlap is minimal
  • An admin scripting an ad-hoc scheduled task that happens to reference a file literally named 1.bat under a user profile
  • Software-deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) staging batch scripts in unusual user folders
  • Red-team/pentest persistence tests mimicking updater task names
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the scheduled task XML (Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName GoogleUpDate) and the 1.bat contents; confirm the task runs as SYSTEM, once, and creates a service. Hash 1.bat against MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a. 2) Contain: Disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and block the loader DLL and its service (see the service-creation UC). 3) Hunt: Sweep the estate for the same task name and for the follow-on services (NgcCIntSvc, Cusrxsrv, etc.) and beacons to the OctLurk C2 domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or CommandLine has "\\Videos\\1.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/LurkProxy service DLL side-load via RegisterService ServiceMain AIInstallation High
Hunts the service-based persistence where a batch script (1.bat / auto.bat) registers a Windows service whose ServiceMain registry value points to the 'RegisterService' export of a loader DLL (oleasapi.dll, msbasesysdc.dll). Detects both the anomalous ServiceMain=RegisterService registry write and the campaign's distinctive service names. Article-specific: legitimate svchost DLL services never name their entry point 'RegisterService'. Rationale: Uses the exact loader DLL names (oleasapi.dll, msbasesysdc.dll), the anomalous ServiceMain export 'RegisterService', and the clearly-malicious service names (NgcCIntSvc, Cusrxsrv, specitsrc, cmtastsvc). ServiceMain naming its entry point RegisterService is not a legitimate pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://www.cryptika.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog-steal-passwords-and-control-government-computers/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vendor product legitimately naming a service ServiceDll export 'RegisterService' (rare but possible for custom svchost DLL services)
  • Hyper-V integration services (vmic*) and PNRPHostSvc are legitimate names — excluded here to avoid FPs, only the non-standard names are matched
  • Endpoint agents that write to Services keys during install (match narrowed to the two loader DLL names)
  • Backup/imaging tools that re-create service registry keys during restore
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Open the flagged service registry key, note the ServiceDll path and hash the DLL (compare to oleasapi.dll 082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069). Identify the parent process that wrote the key (1.bat/auto.bat/cmd.exe). 2) Contain: Stop and delete the service, quarantine the loader DLL, isolate the host — the loader reflectively injects the backdoor into memory so a memory capture before reboot is valuable. 3) Hunt: Search for the sibling service names across the fleet and for beacons to the campaign C2 (next UC); pull the batch scripts to find the admin credentials used for remote task/service creation.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceMain" and RegistryValueData =~ "RegisterService")
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceDll" and RegistryValueData has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceName in~ ("NgcCIntSvc","Cusrxsrv","specitsrc","cmtastsvc")
    or ServiceFileName has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections to the hard-coded OctLurk, SilkLurk and LurkProxy C2 domains and IP addresses over TLS/443 (and the LurkProxy connectivity pre-check to dns.ssentialserv.xyz -> 154.196.162.76). Article-specific: these are the exact backdoor domains/IPs published in the Kaspersky IOC set. Rationale: Exact FQDNs and IPs from the published IOC list, matched on full hostnames (not the parent dynamic-DNS providers gleeze.com/kozow.com) to avoid collateral. Includes the LurkProxy pre-check domain dns.ssentialserv.xyz -> 154.196.162.76. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com resembles the legitimate Leroy Merlin retailer domain — verify the resolved IP against the IOC list before escalating on that hostname alone
  • Shared hosting / VPS IPs (Vultr/Choopa ranges like 95.179.x, 45.77.x) may later be reassigned to benign tenants — decays over time
  • Security scanners or threat-intel enrichment tools deliberately resolving IOC domains
  • An analyst workstation browsing to the IOCs during investigation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in (c2Ips)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process for the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect svchost.exe hosting the malicious service, or a LurkProxy process. Confirm TLS/443 and beaconing cadence. 2) Contain: Block the domains/IPs at the proxy and perimeter firewall, isolate any beaconing host. 3) Hunt: For each host, pivot to the loader service and GoogleUpDate task UCs, and check for LurkProxy listening on port 64980 and follow-on tooling (fscan, secretsdump, Pandora RC agent).
let c2Domains = dynamic(["dns.multitoconference.com","tj.tajikistandip.com","fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com","confbase.mdpsupport.net","digital.leroymerlin.com","api2.annoyingremote.com","about.blsouqs.com","ssl.blsouqs.com","dns.ssentialserv.xyz","tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com","wedfcvbn.gleeze.com","rgnojb.casacam.net","ctyuhjerf.kozow.com","uyhvfredc.accesscam.org","gycudore.kozow.com"]);
let c2Ips = dynamic(["45.138.157.165","154.196.162.76","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (c2Domains) or RemoteIP in (c2Ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["dns.multitoconference.com","tj.tajikistandip.com","fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com","confbase.mdpsupport.net","digital.leroymerlin.com","api2.annoyingremote.com","about.blsouqs.com","ssl.blsouqs.com","dns.ssentialserv.xyz","tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com","wedfcvbn.gleeze.com","rgnojb.casacam.net","ctyuhjerf.kozow.com","uyhvfredc.accesscam.org","gycudore.kozow.com"]);
let c2Ips = dynamic(["45.138.157.165","154.196.162.76","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"]);
union
 (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery in~ (c2Domains) | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DnsQuery, EvtType="DNS"),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (c2Ips) | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, Src=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, EvtType="NetConn")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OctLurk SilkLurk LurkProxy C2 Network Connection
id: b3d7e219-8a44-4c60-9f1b-2e6c0d4a7f51

detection:

      - '45.138.157.165'

      - '45.77.136.228'

source:windows.sysmon (@DestinationHostname:(dns.multitoconference.com OR tj.tajikistandip.com OR fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com OR confbase.mdpsupport.net OR digital.leroymerlin.com OR api2.annoyingremote.com OR about.blsouqs.com OR ssl.blsouqs.com OR dns.ssentialserv.xyz OR tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com OR wedfcvbn.gleeze.com OR rgnojb.casacam.net OR ctyuhjerf.kozow.com OR uyhvfredc.accesscam.org OR gycudore.kozow.com) OR @DestinationIp:(45.138.157.165 OR 154.196.162.76 OR 95.179.210.138 OR 45.77.136.228 OR 95.179.141.26 OR 45.32.152.50 OR 212.11.39.138 OR 195.86.120.2 OR 154.196.187.73 OR 45.61.149.112 OR 64.7.198.130))

OctLurk Command Shell plugin post-compromise recon cluster (chcp 1256 + session enum) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the OctLurk Command Shell plugin's post-compromise reconnaissance: it launches cmd.exe and runs chcp 1256 (Arabic code page), powershell $PSVersionTable, qwinsta, klist sessions and TASKLIST /V. Fires when three or more of these article-specific recon commands cluster on one host within an hour. The chcp 1256 switch is a strong differentiator tying the activity to this actor's Syria-targeting operations. Rationale: Anchors on the exact recon commands from the article's Command Shell plugin table (chcp 1256, qwinsta, klist sessions, TASKLIST /V, $PSVersionTable). chcp 1256 (Arabic code page) on a Central Asian government host is highly unusual; requiring 3+ distinct commands in an hour suppresses one-off admin use. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1614.001 T1033 T1057
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin or helpdesk running qwinsta/tasklist/klist during legitimate session or Kerberos troubleshooting
  • Logon scripts or monitoring agents that enumerate sessions and processes on a schedule
  • Legitimately Arabic-locale machines where chcp 1256 is set by the OS (rare in Central Asia targets)
  • Software inventory tooling querying $PSVersionTable during discovery
Suppression filter
| where Parents !has "mmc.exe" and not (Parents has "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the parent chain of the recon commands — OctLurk drives them via a cmd.exe launched by svchost.exe hosting the malicious service. Legitimate admin recon usually descends from an interactive shell/RDP session. 2) Contain: If the parent is a suspicious svchost/service, isolate the host and proceed to the service and C2 UCs. 3) Hunt: Look for follow-on credential access (secretsdump, browser password stealer), fscan network scanning, keylogger drops, and Pandora RC agent remote-access installs on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "chcp.com" and ProcessCommandLine has "1256")
    or FileName =~ "qwinsta.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "klist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "sessions")
    or (FileName =~ "tasklist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/V")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize DistinctCmds = dcount(FileName), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine),
            Parents = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctCmds >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\chcp.com" and CommandLine has "1256")
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\qwinsta.exe"
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\klist.exe" and CommandLine has "sessions")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\tasklist.exe" and CommandLine has "/V")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize DistinctCmds = dcount(NewProcessName), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctCmds >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\chcp.com OR *\\CHCP.COM) AND @CommandLine:*1256*) OR @Image:(*\\qwinsta.exe OR *\\QWINSTA.EXE) OR (@Image:(*\\klist.exe OR *\\KLIST.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*sessions*) OR (@Image:(*\\tasklist.exe OR *\\TASKLIST.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*\/V*) OR @CommandLine:*$PSVersionTable*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ((ImageFileName=/\\chcp\.com$/i AND CommandLine=/1256/) OR ImageFileName=/\\qwinsta\.exe$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\klist\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/sessions/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\tasklist\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s\/V/i) OR CommandLine=/\$PSVersionTable/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true), as=distinct_cmds)
| distinct_cmds >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as commands dc(Processes.process_name) as distinct_cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chcp.com AND Processes.process="*1256*") OR Processes.process_name=qwinsta.exe OR (Processes.process_name=klist.exe AND Processes.process="*sessions*") OR (Processes.process_name=tasklist.exe AND Processes.process="*/V*") OR Processes.process="*$PSVersionTable*" by Processes.dest _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where distinct_cmds>=3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as commands dc(Processes.process_name) as distinct_cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chcp.com AND Processes.process="*1256*") OR Processes.process_name=qwinsta.exe OR (Processes.process_name=klist.exe AND Processes.process="*sessions*") OR (Processes.process_name=tasklist.exe AND Processes.process="*/V*") OR Processes.process="*$PSVersionTable*" by Processes.dest _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where distinct_cmds>=3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.138.157.165", "154.196.162.76", "95.179.210.138", "45.77.136.228", "95.179.141.26", "45.32.152.50", "212.11.39.138", "195.86.120.2", "154.196.187.73", "45.61.149.112", "64.7.198.130") or RemoteUrl has_any ("dns.multitoconference.com", "tj.tajikistandip.com", "fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com", "confbase.mdpsupport.net", "digital.leroymerlin.com", "api2.annoyingremote.com", "about.blsouqs.com", "ssl.blsouqs.com", "dns.ssentialserv.xyz", "tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["45.138.157.165", "154.196.162.76", "95.179.210.138", "45.77.136.228", "95.179.141.26", "45.32.152.50", "212.11.39.138", "195.86.120.2", "154.196.187.73", "45.61.149.112", "64.7.198.130"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["dns.multitoconference.com", "tj.tajikistandip.com", "fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com", "confbase.mdpsupport.net", "digital.leroymerlin.com", "api2.annoyingremote.com", "about.blsouqs.com", "ssl.blsouqs.com", "dns.ssentialserv.xyz", "tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com"]);
ImNetworkSession

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069", "f4578e869a735cfad691f927bae3e638", "7c2f64461bb519c6cbf1fc687675514c", "8269d6ba1b6842f9152c90cf7add9b93", "3c9a1ba8e0c7475706adc6376e9d7b7c", "ef59aad625eebda8650aec5820d6ce69", "a0cc7accc79abb0287aaba825d0351f0", "a56cce62930a6bee80d679b4c495a340", "1415a78b75de7db4ba3d1e61d7db4501", "a4d550a3ba0cd073fe3839b99d98a7a8", "32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927", "2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f", "37dc84e4bcad92fa28f1e7778d088283", "cf903e4a1629aa0582fd0363b5786676", "18dc8bff47cc282508354771d0c8cf8c", "9a1dd1d96481d61934dcc2d568971d06", "6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a", "b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6", "45cf5916fab4272a1313c26e67aa9220", "4e6d5c4770d5a822d7fcce6a74f7ad73", "5e26df131ff0a679a0a2699b723b46e3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'

falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without Prompts

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 18 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

South Korean authorities and four security firms have disclosed a state-sponsored campaign that compromised trusted domestic websites. The attackers used those sites to exploit locally installed financial-security software and infect targeted visitors with SIGNBT or COPPERHEDGE backdoors. A compromised page could infect a system running a vulnerable AnySign4PC version without a prompt or

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Exploit-script delivery from watering-hole domain jshosting.me · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AnySign4PC watering-hole exploit dropping malicious DLL to user-writable path · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] net.tmp / inet.tmp loader execution shared across espionage and Gunra chains · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Injected SyncHost.exe writing encrypted C2 config blob under Services registry key · [LLM] Reverse SSH tunnel / outbound to known C2 176.65.128.26 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic evidence destruction via SDelete and CCleaner · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
AnySign4PC watering-hole exploit dropping malicious DLL to user-writable path AIExploitation High
Hunts the AnySign4PC financial-security process (vulnerable 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6) writing an unexpected DLL to a user-writable directory — the drive-by chain in which a compromised page triggers a WebSocket buffer overflow and the exploited program 'generates an error and creates a malicious DLL without a download prompt.' A signed certificate-signing utility writing a DLL into Temp/AppData/Public is not normal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's specific product name (AnySign4PC) and the reported behaviour that the exploited security program creates a malicious DLL with no user interaction; a signed e-signature utility writing DLLs to user-writable paths is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/
ATT&CKT1189 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AnySign4PC legitimate self-update writing an updated module into ProgramData
  • Certificate plug-in installer extracting helper DLLs during a genuine e-signing session
  • EDR/AV quarantine-restore placing an AnySign DLL back under AppData
  • Software-packaging/repackaging tooling capturing AnySign install to AppData
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\ProgramData\AnySign" and SHA256 in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped DLL (SHA256) and check its signer/prevalence; confirm the host's AnySign4PC version is 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6 via software inventory. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill AnySign4PC, and delete the vulnerable installation per KISA guidance (upgrade to 1.1.5.0). 3) Hunt: pivot to any child injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe, encrypted registry blobs under Services keys, and outbound SSH to 176.65.128.26 on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "AnySign"
| where FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "AnySign"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected SyncHost.exe writing encrypted C2 config blob under Services registry key AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE storing encrypted command-and-control configuration as binary blobs under service-registry entries after injecting into the legitimate Microsoft SyncHost.exe. SyncHost.exe (a user-context sync host) writing binary values under HKLM ...\Services is anomalous and matches the 'reads C2 information from the Windows registry' and 'encrypted registry blobs' findings. Rationale: Uses the article's reported injection target (SyncHost.exe, shared by both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains) plus the S2W/AhnLab finding of encrypted registry blobs under service-registry entries; SyncHost.exe touching HKLM Services is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1112 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive/Office sync component legitimately updating a per-service config value
  • Endpoint management agent writing service parameters via a sync host process
  • Windows servicing operations reconfiguring a service after an update
  • Third-party sync tool that reuses the SyncHost.exe name writing benign service settings
Suppression filter
| where RegistryKey !has "\Services\OneSyncSvc" and RegistryKey !has "\Services\OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the written RegistryKey/value and confirm SyncHost.exe's parent and image path; verify the process was code-injected (unexpected loaded modules, no signed OneDrive parentage). 2) Contain: isolate host, snapshot the registry value for decryption, and suspend the injected process. 3) Hunt: correlate with AnySign4PC DLL drop, net.tmp/inet.tmp loaders, and beacons to 176.65.128.26 on the same device.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SyncHost.exe"
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueSetCreated")
| where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","None")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "SyncHost.exe"
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where RegistryValueType has "Binary"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reverse SSH tunnel / outbound to known C2 176.65.128.26 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the reverse-tunnelling address 176.65.128[.]26 used across both the SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE espionage chain and the Gunra ransomware intrusions. Any egress to this hardcoded IOC — especially over SSH (22) — is a confirmed C2 signal. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted IOC IP 176.65.128.26, explicitly named as the reverse-tunnelling address reused across both operations — a static, high-fidelity network indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample from the corporate range
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanner appliance actively probing the IOC
  • Shared-hosting reuse if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and port (SSH/22 = reverse tunnel); pull the full connection history to this IP org-wide. 2) Contain: block 176.65.128.26 at the egress firewall and isolate any connecting host. 3) Hunt: on connecting hosts look for ssh.exe/plink tunnels, the SSH key fingerprint Qr1to32lQHxEu6phzNyrTZrU0iElrOfVWMBLnqoen24, and injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "176.65.128.26"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

net.tmp / inet.tmp loader execution shared across espionage and Gunra chains AIInstallation High
Hunts execution or loading of the malware filenames net.tmp and inet.tmp — the shared loader artefacts AhnLab found in both the state-sponsored and Gunra ransomware chains (inet.tmp used an identical argument, net.tmp arguments in a GUID format). Typically loaded via a LOLBin (rundll32/regsvr32) referencing the .tmp module. Rationale: Uses the exact shared malware filenames net.tmp and inet.tmp named by AhnLab as cross-operation overlap evidence; .tmp modules referenced on a command line via LOLBins are unusual and article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1055.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installer temporarily naming a payload net.tmp/inet.tmp during extraction
  • Backup/AV product using .tmp scratch files with coincidental names
  • Custom in-house tooling that stages temp files with net-prefixed names
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the .tmp file, the loading LOLBin, and the GUID-format argument; hash and detonate if unknown. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the .tmp before the actor's rename-to-4-char/delete anti-forensics fires. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same GUID argument on other hosts, AnySign4PC DLL drops, and beacons to 176.65.128.26.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploit-script delivery from watering-hole domain jshosting.me AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS/HTTP resolution of jshosting[.]me, the domain AhnLab found distributing exploit scripts in both the espionage and Gunra attack sets. A host resolving this domain indicates contact with the watering-hole exploit-delivery infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted IOC domain jshosting.me, explicitly named as the exploit-script distribution domain in both attack sets — a static, high-fidelity delivery indicator. Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the process (browser vs. AnySign4PC/security software) and whether an exploit followed. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block jshosting.me at DNS and egress; isolate hosts that resolved it near an AnySign4PC error. 3) Hunt: on those hosts look for the AnySign4PC DLL drop, net.tmp/inet.tmp loaders, and injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe.

Anti-forensic evidence destruction via SDelete and CCleaner AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the actors' evidence-destruction step observed by Plainbit — SDelete and CCleaner used to securely wipe artefacts (accompanying the rename-malicious-files-to-random-4-character-names-before-deletion procedure). Execution of these secure-deletion tools on a workstation involved in the campaign is a strong post-compromise cleanup signal. Rationale: Uses the specific anti-forensic tooling (SDelete, CCleaner) named by Plainbit for evidence destruction in this campaign; pairs well as a corroborating pivot when other campaign IOCs are present on the host. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin decommissioning/wiping a device before reissue
  • Privacy-conscious user running CCleaner for routine cleanup
  • Sysinternals SDelete used to wipe free space during legitimate data-sanitisation
  • Disposal/asset-retirement workflow securely wiping drives
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccsetup.exe","msiexec.exe") and AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user context (non-machine account), the parent process, and whether campaign IOCs (AnySign4PC DLL, net.tmp, 176.65.128.26) exist on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve volume snapshots/journals before further wiping; capture $MFT and USN journal for rename-then-delete evidence. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for FileRenamed events producing random four-character names immediately preceding FileDeleted on the same host.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sdelete","ccleaner")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("sdelete","ccleaner")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceFileEvents

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

SilverFox DLL side-loading: PDFCORE8.dll loaded by ConvertToPDF.exe / PDFDirect.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the SilverFox ValleyRAT loader stage where the malicious PDFCORE8.dll is side-loaded by the legitimate Zeon Corporation binaries ConvertToPDF.exe or PDFDirect.exe. This is the self-contained execution framework that embeds the three BYOVD drivers, so catching the sideload catches the whole chain at install time. Rationale: PDFCORE8.dll is a bespoke malicious DLL name paired to two specific legitimate Zeon binaries (ConvertToPDF.exe/PDFDirect.exe) reported by Cato and corroborated by SC Media/SecurityAffairs — the exe+dll pairing is unique to this campaign and near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/silver-fox-group-uses-new-drivers-in-byovd-attacks-against-japanese-manufacturer • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Zeon Corporation PDF software genuinely installed and loading its own vendor-signed PDFCORE8.dll from Program Files
  • Software packaging/repackaging test lab copying Zeon binaries to a staging path
  • EDR replaying quarantined samples during a controlled detonation
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the load path — legit Zeon software installs under Program Files; a load from Downloads/Temp/ZIP-extract path or an unsigned PDFCORE8.dll is malicious. Check the DLL SHA256 against VT. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect process tree, and quarantine PDFCORE8.dll plus any co-located .sys files. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for BootRepair.sys/EnPortv.sys/wsftprm.sys drops, scheduled-task watchdog persistence, and outbound traffic to 43.128.26.132.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Loader = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          LoaderPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          Dll = FileName, DllPath = FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe") or isempty(ActingProcessName)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilverFox 3-driver BYOVD: BootRepair.sys / EnPortv.sys / wsftprm.sys dropped to disk AIInstallation High
Detects the write of the vulnerable drivers embedded in the SilverFox loader (BootRepair.sys, EnPortv.sys, wsftprm.sys, plus the earlier amsdk.sys) used as a plug-and-play BYOVD framework to gain kernel access and impair security controls. These driver filenames are the sharpest campaign IOC. Rationale: BootRepair.sys and EnPortv.sys are newly-attributed SilverFox drivers (Zeon-signed) not seen in prior waves, and wsftprm.sys/amsdk.sys are the known SilverFox vulnerable drivers — all confirmed by Cato and secondary reporting; matching these exact filenames on write is high-fidelity BYOVD staging. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/silver-fox-group-uses-new-drivers-in-byovd-attacks-against-japanese-manufacturer
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host that genuinely runs WS_FTP (wsftprm.sys) or a legitimate boot-repair/port-virtualization utility installing its own signed driver
  • Vulnerability researchers or red team detonating BYOVD samples in a lab
  • Backup/imaging software bundling a boot-repair driver
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check the writing process and drop path — a driver written by ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect/PDFCORE8-spawned process or to a temp/user path is malicious; verify the driver hash and signer. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, block the driver hash, and check whether the service was already loaded (kernel access may already be established) — plan for offline remediation. Step 3 (hunt): Look for co-located PDFCORE8.dll side-load, security-process termination events, NTDLL unhooking artifacts, and C2 to 43.128.26.132.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys","EnPortv.sys","wsftprm.sys","amsdk.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          WrittenBy = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          WriterPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys","EnPortv.sys","wsftprm.sys","amsdk.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilverFox ValleyRAT C2 / shellcode fetch to 43.128.26.132 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any outbound connection to the SilverFox loader's external server 43.128.26.132, which is contacted to fetch the shellcode later injected into svchost.exe (ValleyRAT). A single confirmed campaign C2 IP, so any hit is high-severity. Rationale: 43.128.26.132 is the explicit external server the SilverFox loader contacts to retrieve injected shellcode, named in the article and Cato write-up — a discrete C2 IOC that warrants alerting on any egress. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanning/sandbox infrastructure inside your org deliberately probing the IP
  • Security researcher connecting to the C2 for analysis from a corporate host
  • IP reassigned to benign hosting after takedown (validate first-seen date vs reassignment)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process — a connection from svchost.exe with an anomalous parent, or from a PDF-loader process, confirms the ValleyRAT chain. Capture the process tree and any bytes transferred (shellcode pull). Step 2 (contain): Block 43.128.26.132 at the firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and kill the initiating process. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for connections to the IP, then pivot to PDFCORE8.dll side-loads, BYOVD driver drops, and scheduled-task watchdog persistence on affected hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "43.128.26.132"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "43.128.26.132"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, SrcUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
