ValleyRAT thread-context-hijack svchost.exe spawned by non-services.exe parent AIInstallation Medium
Detects a new svchost.exe process created by a parent other than services.exe — the anomaly produced when the SilverFox loader spawns a fresh svchost.exe and injects ValleyRAT shellcode via thread-context hijacking. Legitimate svchost is always a child of services.exe, so an off-tree svchost is a strong injection signal. Rationale: The article states shellcode is injected into a newly created svchost.exe via thread-context hijacking; a svchost.exe whose parent is not services.exe is the observable side-effect of that off-tree spawn and is a well-established injection tell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/
ATT&CKT1055.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe or .NET ngen spawning svchost-like helpers
  • Sysinternals/EDR tooling launching svchost for diagnostics
  • Third-party installers briefly invoking svchost.exe -k during setup
  • RDP/WinRM admin sessions launching service host helpers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("C:\\Windows\\System32","C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64") or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","wininit.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the parent — a PDF-loader, script host, or unsigned binary parenting svchost.exe is malicious; confirm the svchost path is the real System32/SysWOW64 image (masquerading if not). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and suspend/kill the svchost child and its parent loader before ValleyRAT establishes recovery. Step 3 (hunt): Because of the dual watchdog, also find and remove the scheduled-task watchdog and the loader — check for PDFCORE8.dll, BYOVD driver drops, and C2 to 43.128.26.132; expect relaunch if either component survives.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","MsMpEng.exe","ngen.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

let LookbackDays = 7d;

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Hermes Agent Langflow exploit + FOFA enumeration tooling (langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py, CVE-2026-33017) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Claude Code / Codex anti-attribution and skip-permission config (knaithe AI tooling)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Connection to code.newcli.com — anti-attribution AI-coding-tool proxy (knaithe/KnYuan) · [LLM] Server/non-browser process calling native Chinese LLM APIs (api.deepseek.com / dashscope.aliyuncs.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Connection to code.newcli.com — anti-attribution AI-coding-tool proxy (knaithe/KnYuan) AICommand & Control High
Hunts host/network traffic to code.newcli[.]com, the third-party proxy the actor routed Claude Code (/ultra) and Codex (/codex/v1) through to reduce traceability. Any enterprise endpoint resolving or connecting to this domain indicates a host running the campaign's proxied Western AI-coding tooling. Rationale: code.newcli[.]com is a hard IOC named in Unit 42's Table 1 as the proxy for both Western tools (/ultra and /codex/v1 paths). A fixed attacker-owned proxy domain is a near-zero-FP network indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A red-team/pentest team internally trialing the same code.newcli.com proxy service
  • Security researcher replicating the Unit 42 campaign in a lab connected to corp DNS
  • Threat-intel analyst intentionally resolving the IOC to enrich a case
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ platform generating a synthetic resolution log for the blocked domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-enrich.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the resolving host and the InitiatingProcess — confirm whether it's an AI-coding-tool binary (claude, codex, node) vs a browser; pull the full command line and folder path. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block newcli.com at the proxy/DNS/firewall, and revoke any API keys/tokens found in the tool's config. Step 3 (hunt): On the same host search for the anti-attribution env vars (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER, disable_response_storage), connections to api.deepseek.com / dashscope.aliyuncs.com, and any langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py execution.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "newcli.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "code.newcli.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "newcli.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCodeName, ServerIPAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Server/non-browser process calling native Chinese LLM APIs (api.deepseek.com / dashscope.aliyuncs.com) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts non-browser processes reaching the DeepSeek and Alibaba DashScope (Qwen/GLM/Kimi/MiniMax) native API endpoints the actor called directly for autonomous reasoning and code generation. A server, python, or agent process talking to these LLM APIs indicates automated offensive AI tooling running in the environment. Rationale: api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com are the direct native API endpoints named in Table 1 for DeepSeek/Hermes and Qwen Code. Filtering to non-browser initiators isolates automated agent tooling from casual human LLM use; the Sentinel DNS variant can't see the process, so it is DNS-only and broader (noted). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/

  • CI/CD pipeline or automation server calling DeepSeek API for a business feature

  • Third-party software with an embedded Qwen/DeepSeek integration

Correlate with the host's DeepSeek/Qwen config files and API keys. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host and rotate/disable the discovered API key; block the endpoints at egress for non-approved hosts. Step 3 (hunt): Look for co-located Hermes Agent artifacts (godmode/fofa skills), fofoapi.py, langflow_poc.py, and connections to code.newcli.com on the same or peer hosts.

Claude Code / Codex anti-attribution and skip-permission config (knaithe AI tooling) AIInstallation High
Hunts process command lines and config-file writes that set the actor's anti-attribution and safety-bypass options: CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1, dangerously-skip-permissions, and Codex disable_response_storage=true. These settings are the signature of AI-coding tools deliberately configured to reduce traceability and remove execution guardrails. Rationale: The four config strings are quoted verbatim in Unit 42's Table 1 as the actor's anti-attribution / guardrail-removal settings. They are highly specific to deliberately-abused AI-coding tooling and would rarely appear in benign command lines. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1070
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running Claude Code with dangerously-skip-permissions in a throwaway sandbox
  • Security researcher reproducing the Unit 42 config for analysis
  • CI job setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 to reduce telemetry in an air-gapped build
  • Internal AI-tooling team benchmarking Codex with disable_response_storage for privacy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ci-runner.exe","buildagent.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full command line and parent process; confirm whether the tool is sanctioned and who the account owner is. Check the host for a matching config file (settings.json / config.toml). Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host, capture the AI-tool config and any exploit-dev directories, and revoke discovered API keys/proxy creds. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to network traffic to code.newcli.com and api.deepseek.com/dashscope.aliyuncs.com from the same host, and search for Hermes Agent skills and langflow_poc.py/fofoapi.py.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

Hermes Agent Langflow exploit + FOFA enumeration tooling (langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py, CVE-2026-33017) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts execution of the actor's autonomous exploit and asset-enumeration scripts: the Langflow CVE-2026-33017 PoC scanner (langflow_poc.py --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10) and the fofoapi.py FOFA internet-asset-search helper driving the fofa-cyberspace-search skill. Presence indicates a host used to run the Hermes Agent autonomous attack cycle. Rationale: langflow_poc.py --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10 and fofoapi.py are literal command/script names from the article's Phase 1 attack flow and the fofa-cyberspace-search skill. These filenames are unique to this tooling and essentially never appear in benign activity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1590 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned red-team running the same public Langflow PoC during an authorized engagement
  • Vulnerability-research team reproducing CVE-2026-33017 in a lab
  • Blue-team analyst detonating the PoC to build detections
  • Security tool bundling a copy of langflow_poc.py for scanning inventory
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-" and DeviceName !startswith "LAB-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the executing host and account, the parent process (python/agent), and whether --scan-file/langflow_targets.txt indicates outbound scanning of external targets. Determine if this is an authorized engagement. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorized, isolate the host, block outbound scanning egress, and preserve the exploit-dev directory, target list, and FOFA API keys. Step 3 (hunt): Search the host and peers for Hermes Agent skills (godmode, web-terminal-exploitation, fofa-cyberspace-search), the FofaMap-Platinum MCP server, connections to code.newcli.com / api.deepseek.com, and the other campaign CVEs (CVE-2026-21858, CVE-2025-68613, CVE-2026-3055, CVE-2026-39987, CVE-2026-34486, CVE-2026-33824).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow_poc.py","langflow_targets.txt","fofoapi.py")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "langflow_poc" and ProcessCommandLine has "--scan-file")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("langflow_poc.py","langflow_targets.txt","fofoapi.py")
   or (CommandLine has "langflow_poc" and CommandLine has "--scan-file")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"

        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Kaspersky experts dissect GenieLocker: new custom ransomware variants for Windows, Linux, and ESXi systems. We found this family in attacks by Toy Ghouls, a financially motivated extortion group.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1021.002 T1190 T1204.002 T1486

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Toy Ghouls’ new toy: the GenieLocker ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Toy Ghouls toolset staging: SoftPerfect netscan, socks5.exe proxy, Mimikatz · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Toy Ghouls C2: egress to 89.125.66.101, socks5.exe proxy, reverse SSH tunnel · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GenieLocker Windows PE encryptor: secret hex arg + genie_encrypt --percent/--recursive flags · [LLM] GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi: genie_encrypt CLI execution · [LLM] KeePassXC credential-vault access by non-KeePass process (.kdbx theft) · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change
GenieLocker Windows PE encryptor: secret hex arg + genie_encrypt --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the GenieLocker Windows ransomware binary, which requires a long hex 'secret argument' as its first parameter and exposes the distinctive genie_encrypt CLI (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log). Anchored on the confirmed Windows MD5 and the unique long-form flag combination that no legitimate tool shares. Rationale: Uses the confirmed Windows MD5 (5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c) plus the genie_encrypt help-screen flags (--percent/--recursive/--log) and the mandatory hex 'secret argument' pattern extracted from the article and screenshot genielocker1.png. The long-form flag pairing is unique to this family. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/07/29164506/genielocker1.png
ATT&CKT1486 T1480.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/archive utilities that accept a --recursive flag but not alongside --percent
  • Custom internal file-processing scripts using -p and -r short flags coincidentally
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
  • Data-migration tools invoked with long hex job IDs as the first positional argument
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","robocopy.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent process; confirm the hex first-argument + --percent/--recursive shape and check MD5 against 5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c. Note the encryption target path passed as the last argument. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately, kill the process tree, and preserve the log file specified by -l/--log for the secret argument value. 3) Hunt: search for the same binary/flags deployed by PsExec/PAExec across other hosts (mass-deployment), and pivot to C2 IP 89.125.66.101 and KeePassXC/.kdbx access on the same accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where MD5 == "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b[0-9a-f]{32,}\b\s+(-p|--percent)\s+\d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where (MD5 =~ "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c")
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--log")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b[0-9a-f]{32,}\b\s+(-p|--percent)\s+\d"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, MD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi: genie_encrypt CLI execution AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ELF build of GenieLocker used to encrypt Linux servers and ESXi datastore disks after stopping running VMs. Anchored on the same cross-platform genie_encrypt usage string and --percent/--recursive/--log flags observed in the binary help output. Rationale: The help-screen usage string 'genie_encrypt [options] [path]' and the -p/-r/-l flags (image genielocker1.png) are shared by the ELF build, which the article states was used to stop VMs and encrypt ESXi/Linux disks. genie_encrypt as a command token is a near-unique anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/amp/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/07/29164506/genielocker1.png
ATT&CKT1486 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal tool literally named genie_encrypt (extremely unlikely)
  • Backup jobs invoking a recursive percentage-based sampler
  • Admin running a disk utility with --recursive on ESXi shell for maintenance
  • Security team replaying the ELF sample in an isolated lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the affected ESXi/Linux host, capture the full command line and the last positional path argument (encryption target) and confirm running-VM state changes preceding it. 2) Contain: isolate the host/datastore, halt the process, and protect ESXi snapshots/backups from the same actor. 3) Hunt: check for SSH lateral movement into other Linux/ESXi hosts, the reverse SSH tunnel to 89.125.66.101, and the same genie_encrypt invocation across the cluster.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "genie_encrypt"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "genie_encrypt"
   or (SyslogMessage has "--percent" and SyslogMessage has "--recursive")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toy Ghouls C2: egress to 89.125.66.101, socks5.exe proxy, reverse SSH tunnel AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts command-and-control activity from the GenieLocker intrusion: outbound connections to the confirmed C2 IP 89.125.66.101, execution of the dropped socks5.exe proxy, and reverse SSH tunnels (ssh -R) used to reach the C2. Anchored on the article's named C2 IP and tooling. Rationale: Uses the article's single named C2 IP (89.125.66.101) plus the named intrusion tooling socks5.exe and the reverse SSH tunnel (ssh -R) described in the Lateral Movement/C2 section. A hardcoded C2 IP match is alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/
ATT&CKT1090 T1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned pentest reusing socks5 tooling
  • Legit SSH remote-forward (-R) set up by an admin for a service tunnel
  • Threat-intel/EDR sensor sandbox reaching the IOC IP during analysis
  • Shared-hosting IP reassignment causing benign traffic to 89.125.66.101
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-backup","svc-monitor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user for the connection to 89.125.66.101; confirm socks5.exe/ssh -R presence and location. 2) Contain: block the C2 IP at the perimeter, isolate the host, and kill the proxy/tunnel process. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts that resolved or connected to the C2, look for socks5.exe/OpenSSH drops elsewhere, and correlate with GenieLocker execution and PsExec/PAExec deployment.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.125.66.101"
   or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "socks5.exe"
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-R")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.125.66.101"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, SrcUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toy Ghouls toolset staging: SoftPerfect netscan, socks5.exe proxy, Mimikatz AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the post-access tooling the actor deployed for discovery and credential dumping: SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe), the socks5.exe proxy, and Mimikatz. Anchored on the specific tool names/commands named in the Discovery and Credential Access section. Rationale: Directly uses the named discovery/credential tools from the article: SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe), socks5.exe, and Mimikatz (matched by classic module commands and the gentilkiwi signature to survive renames). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1046 T1003.001 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/network team legitimately running SoftPerfect Network Scanner for inventory
  • Red-team engagement using Mimikatz with authorization
  • Renamed penetration-testing socks proxy used by sanctioned testers
  • EDR/AV quarantine event re-surfacing an old Mimikatz sample name
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "netscan.exe" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-netops","netadmin"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether netscan.exe/socks5.exe/Mimikatz execution was authorized (change ticket / pentest window); capture user, host, and drop path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, reset credentials for any account active on it, and remove the staged binaries. 3) Hunt: pivot to KeePassXC/.kdbx access by the same accounts, RDP/SSH lateral movement, and any subsequent PsExec/PAExec deployment of genie_encrypt.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("netscan.exe","socks5.exe")
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "gentilkiwi"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","privilege::debug","lsadump::")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("netscan.exe","socks5.exe")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","privilege::debug","lsadump::")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("netscan.exe","socks5.exe") OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa::*" OR Processes.process="*privilege::debug*" OR Processes.process="*lsadump::*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

KeePassXC credential-vault access by non-KeePass process (.kdbx theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts attempts to steal stored credentials from KeePassXC databases, which the actor accessed on multiple compromised hosts. Flags creation/copy/rename of .kdbx vault files by any process other than the KeePass client — the shape of a database being staged for exfil or opened by attacker tooling. Rationale: Anchored on the article's statement that the actor accessed KeePassXC databases on several hosts to extract stored credentials; .kdbx touched by anything other than the KeePass client is a high-fidelity vault-theft signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/
ATT&CKT1555.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup software (Veeam, robocopy, OneDrive/Dropbox sync) copying a user's .kdbx
  • User manually copying their vault to a USB/network share
  • IT migrating a profile including the KeePass database
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine engine moving a .kdbx during a scan
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","onedrive.exe","robocopy.exe","dropbox.exe") and ActionType == "FileCreated")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process and account touching the .kdbx and whether it's a known backup/sync tool vs attacker tooling (cmd, powershell, robocopy to a staging dir). 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset every credential known to be stored in that vault. 3) Hunt: correlate with Mimikatz execution on the same host, look for the vault file appearing in temp/staging paths, and check outbound transfer to C2 89.125.66.101.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("keepassxc.exe","keepass.exe","keepassxc-cli.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where ActingProcessName !has "keepass"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: KeePassXC Vault (.kdbx) Access by Non-KeePass Process
id: d15a8e60-2b7c-4f39-b1a4-9e6c0d3f2b18
description: Detects a non-KeePass process creating, modifying, or renaming a .kdbx database file, indicating credential-vault theft as seen in GenieLocker intrusions.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.t1555.005
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.kdbx'
  filter_keepass:
    Image|contains: 'keepass'
  condition: selection and not filter_keepass
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:*.kdbx -@Image:(*\\keepassxc.exe OR *\\KeePassXC.exe OR *\\keepass.exe OR *\\KeePass.exe OR *\\keepassxc-cli.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\.kdbx$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/keepass/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.kdbx" AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("keepassxc.exe","keepass.exe","keepassxc-cli.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.kdbx" AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("keepassxc.exe","keepass.exe","keepassxc-cli.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/

    product: windows
detection:

            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: critical

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("socks5.exe", "config.msi", "kftd.exe", "genie_encrypt.exe", "run.exe", "run2.exe", "genie.exe", "consultant.exe", "tempo.exe", "kernel.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents

| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/vmware/welcome") or FileName in~ ("socks5.exe", "config.msi", "kftd.exe", "genie_encrypt.exe", "run.exe", "run2.exe", "genie.exe", "consultant.exe", "tempo.exe", "kernel.exe"))

          InitiatingProcessCommandLine

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] TA488 half-click OWA lure: inbound generic email with no URLs or attachments · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OWAReaper server-side persistence: Owner rights granted to Default user on mailbox folders · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OWAReaper C2 / DNS-tunneled exfil to TA488 actor-controlled domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

OWAReaper server-side persistence: Owner rights granted to Default user on mailbox folders AIInstallation High
Hunts OWAReaper's key persistence act — granting Owner-level permission to the 'Default' (or 'Anonymous') principal on mailbox folders via the OWA web client, so any authenticated org user retains mailbox access after the victim's credential rotation or device re-image. This is the specific server-side backdoor Proofpoint highlights as requiring deliberate Exchange-side removal. Rationale: Directly targets the article's marquee behaviour — OWAReaper 'grants itself Owner-level permissions to the Default user on every mail folder', producing rare UpdateFolderPermissions/AddFolderPermissions events with Default/Anonymous=Owner via the OWA client. Owner-to-Default is almost never legitimate. Cross-checked Proofpoint and BleepingComputer confirming the server-side persistence mechanism. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-exchange-owa-zero-day-for-long-term-mailbox-access/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/30/cve-2026-42897-microsoft-exchange-email-attack/
ATT&CKT1098.002 T1098
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin or migration tooling bulk-resetting folder permissions during mailbox onboarding
  • Legitimate org-wide calendar/free-busy sharing that sets Default to Reviewer (not Owner — refine on Owner)
  • Third-party mailbox delegation/archiving products writing folder ACLs
  • Help-desk troubleshooting of shared-mailbox access
  • Resource-mailbox (room/equipment) auto-accept configuration
Suppression filter
| where ClientInfoString has "OWA" or ClientInfoString has "OutlookWebApp" // scope to the web client OWAReaper runs in
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the OfficeActivity/CloudAppEvents record — confirm grantee is Default/Anonymous with Owner rights and that ClientInfoString/UserAgent indicates OWA. Note MailboxOwnerUPN, ClientIP, and the acting UserId. 2) Contain: Remove the malicious folder permission on every affected folder (Set-MailboxFolderPermission ... -User Default -AccessRights None), then check for and revoke any Add-MailboxPermission/delegate grants; force sign-out and revoke OAuth tokens for the mailbox. Because this persists server-side, credential rotation alone is insufficient. 3) Hunt: Enumerate all mailboxes with Default/Anonymous=Owner org-wide, review the same OWA session for OAuth token theft from add-ins with ReadWriteMailbox, and correlate the acting IP to the exfil-domain UC.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in~ ("UpdateFolderPermissions","AddFolderPermissions","ModifyFolderPermissions","Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "Owner" and (Raw has "Default" or Raw has "Anonymous")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, IPAddress, UserAgent, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in~ ("UpdateFolderPermissions","AddFolderPermissions","ModifyFolderPermissions","Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| extend Details = strcat(tostring(Parameters), " ", tostring(EventData), " ", ClientInfoString)
| where Details has "Owner" and (Details has "Default" or Details has "Anonymous")
| project TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, ClientInfoString, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OWAReaper C2 / DNS-tunneled exfil to TA488 actor-controlled domains AICommand & Control High
Detects host or browser resolution/connection to the four TA488 exfiltration and C2 domains used by OWAReaper for AES-CTR HTTPS exfil and DNS label tunneling. These infrastructure domains are deliberately named to mimic DNS-resolver services (asecdns, dnsrecursive, tdndns) to blend into normal traffic. Rationale: Uses the four concrete actor-controlled domains (asecdns.com, acocdn.com, dnsrecursive.eu, tdndns.com) named as OWAReaper's HTTPS exfil and DNS-tunnel destinations. Exact-domain IOC match is inherently high-fidelity; the DNS-service-mimicking naming is itself a hunt tell. Campaign infrastructure corroborated via Proofpoint and Help Net Security reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/30/cve-2026-42897-microsoft-exchange-email-attack/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation infrastructure resolving the IOCs during analysis
  • Security scanners or DNS sinkholes proactively querying known-bad domains
  • An internal passive-DNS or blocklist-testing tool enumerating IOC lists
  • Typosquat collision where a benign lookalike shares a base string (verify exact FQDN suffix)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the querying host/user and the initiating process (expect a browser running an OWA tab — msedge.exe/chrome.exe). Confirm the exact FQDN and check query volume/length for DNS-tunnel patterns (long, high-entropy labels). 2) Contain: Block the four domains at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat the associated mailbox as compromised — revoke OAuth tokens and sessions. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the same user to the mailbox-folder-permission persistence UC, review OWA session history for the CVE-2026-42897 exploit email, and sweep the org for any other host resolving these domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("asecdns.com","acocdn.com","dnsrecursive.eu","tdndns.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("asecdns.com","acocdn.com","dnsrecursive.eu","tdndns.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TA488 half-click OWA lure: inbound generic email with no URLs or attachments AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the delivery shape of the CVE-2026-42897 half-click campaign — inbound emails deliberately carrying no URLs and no attachments (payload hidden in social-media-icon HTML), using bland informational lures on supply chain, gas/tourism metrics, nuclear energy and public health, frequently from Proton Mail. Hunting-tier scoping for OWA-exposed recipients. Rationale: Encodes the campaign's distinctive delivery signature confirmed by Proofpoint/multiple outlets: zero-URL, zero-attachment inbound mail (the half-click design that excludes links/attachments) with generic lures (semiconductor supply chain, gas markets, tourism, nuclear, public health) and Proton Mail senders. Deliberately hunting-tier given benign text-only mail is common. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/ta488-outlook-half-click-owareaper/
ATT&CKT1566 T1203
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate industry newsletters/analyst briefs on gas, tourism or semiconductor markets with no links
  • Internal or partner informational notices sent as plain text
  • Automated report digests whose subjects contain 'metrics' or 'research update'
  • Proton Mail users legitimately corresponding with the org
  • Marketing preview/plain-text A-B test messages
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("mailchimp.com","sendgrid.net","amazonses.com","mailgun.org")) // strip known bulk-mail ESPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: For hits, prioritise recipients whose mailboxes are OWA/on-prem-Exchange accessible (CVE-2026-42897 targets on-prem OWA). Inspect raw message HTML for onload= handlers and Base64 fragments after '#' inside <img> social-icon elements. 2) Contain: Quarantine/soft-delete matching messages tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, and confirm Exchange is patched for CVE-2026-42897. 3) Hunt: For any recipient who opened the mail in OWA, pivot to the mailbox-folder-permission persistence UC and the actor-domain exfil UC to determine whether OWAReaper executed.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where UrlCount == 0 and AttachmentCount == 0
| where Subject has_any ("supply chain","semiconductor","gas market","gas markets","tourism","nuclear","public health","research update","metrics")
| extend ProtonSender = (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com","pm.me") or SenderFromDomain in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com","pm.me"))
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, ProtonSender, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc

| order by conn_count desc

            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or SHA1 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or MD5 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or SHA1 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or MD5 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Amazon Links Debug and Chalk npm Hijack to North Korea’s Sapphire Sleet

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 13 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Amazon has tied the September 2025 hijack of the npm packages debug and chalk to North Korea. For ten months, the incident sat in the public record as crypto theft: a maintainer phished through a lookalike npm domain and a wallet-draining script pushed into at least 18 packages carrying more than 2 billion weekly downloads between them. The original Aikido and Wiz reports did not attribute the
